title: The Mystery Illness That Explains What We Keep Getting Wrong About Kids
author: Kevin Stinehart
summary: Using the history of pellagra — a devastating nutritional disease misidentified as an infection in the early twentieth-century American South — Kevin Stinehart builds a sustained analogy about how modern adults misread children's visible symptoms while missing underlying causes. Just as early doctors became expert at treating the rash while missing the dietary deficiency that caused it, schools have become very good at naming and treating children's behavioral symptoms — defiance, anxiety, poor executive function — while failing to address the underlying deficit: children are not practicing the basic work of being human. Stinehart, a third-grade teacher, argues that modern childhood has been systematically drained of difficulty: responsibility, boredom, physical risk, open-ended unstructured time, and the experience of beginning something without an adult beside you. The result is children who are loved and capable but under-practiced at independence. The article calls for a systemic rethink of what children need at a foundational level rather than ever-more-refined targeted interventions for the downstream effects.
points: The pellagra analogy is the article's central structural move: early doctors mastered symptom management while missing the nutritional cause, just as modern schools have mastered intervention systems (Tier 2, Tier 3, behavior plans, SEL curricula) while missing the foundational deficit — insufficient practice at being human.

Children today are showing a pattern of symptoms — meltdowns over small frustrations, inability to tolerate boredom, emotional fragility, social immaturity, dependence on adult initiation — that Stinehart argues reflect a systemic deprivation of daily practice in the basic work of independence.

Modern convenience has stripped difficulty from childhood one item at a time: calculators displaced mental arithmetic, GPS displaced navigation, streaming displaced boredom, color-coded bins displaced backpacks, and platforms displaced notebooks — each a small removal of an opportunity to practice capability.

The mistake Stinehart identifies is not that targeted support is wrong but that targeted support has been asked to replace the daily foundational nourishment that all children need. Intervention systems treat the rash; they cannot substitute for the diet.

The insight Goldberger brought to pellagra was a shift of frame: not 'what is attacking these children from outside' but 'what are healthy children getting that sick children lack?' Stinehart argues schools need the same shift — from 'what intervention does this child need' to 'what daily practice is this child missing?'
quotes: At first, the doctors saw the skin. That was the thing nobody could ignore. South Carolina children were showing up with strange, painful rashes on their hands, arms, necks, and faces, especially where the sun touched them.

The doctors looked for contagion. They inspected buildings, bedding, water, air, routines. A mysterious illness moving through orphanages, prisons, asylums, mill villages, and poor Southern communities was spreading, and no one could figure out why.

I think we are staring at visible symptoms and mistaking them for the problem. Teachers see children melting down over small frustrations. Parents see children unable to tolerate boredom. Pediatricians and therapists see anxiety, dysregulation, and emotional fragility.

We call it behavior. Defiance. Attention-seeking. Anxiety. Poor executive function. Weak social skills. Lack of motivation. Immaturity. Those descriptions are not necessarily wrong. A rash really is a rash. A meltdown really is a meltdown. The question is whether we are looking deeply enough.

Schools have become very good at building systems once symptoms appear: Tier 2 supports, Tier 3 interventions, behavior plans, counseling referrals, calming corners, token boards, SEL lessons, small groups, restorative conversations, regulation tools, reward systems, behavior sticker charts, and programs with acronyms that sound like they were named by a tired committee trying to finish before lunch.

Goldberger later pushed the question underneath the visible symptoms. What were sick people eating? What were healthy people eating? The sick were missing nutrients. Scientists later identified vitamin B3 as the specific missing component.
